explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees…” (Luke 12:1). Leaven is what gets worked into dough, and in my line of work I know how far a little bit spreads. Notice He says it first to His disciples, with thousands of people packed around.

Herod is a name that shows up other places in the Gospels (Mark 8:15), but not here. In this verse Jesus says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees…” (Luke 12:1). I think that one is easy to mix up when a warning about leaven is already rolling around in your head. Same dough, different name on the bag.

Jesus doesn't name the Sadducees in this warning. He says, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees…” (Luke 12:1). He even says what that leaven is: “…which is hypocrisy.” Pick the group He actually names, friend.

Yes, baker. Jesus gives the answer Himself: the leaven of the Pharisees is “hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). He doesn't leave His disciples guessing, which I appreciate, because I've guessed wrong on a recipe card before. Hypocrisy is looking one way on the outside while being something else on the inside.

Impatience is a fair guess, since plenty of us rush the oven. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says the leaven of the Pharisees “is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). Hypocrisy is the gap between how someone looks and what's really going on inside.

Laziness is a tempting pick, but Jesus never calls it that. He says the leaven of the Pharisees is “hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). I think of a cookie box with a beautiful lid and nothing inside. That's the picture, friend, looking one way and being another.

Not quite, baker, and here is what Jesus really says: “There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.” (Luke 12:2). Nothing means nothing. No hidden thing gets left out of that sentence.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.” (Luke 12:2). No exceptions on that list. I once tried hiding a burnt batch under a dish towel, and the smell told on me before the timer even stopped.

That's it, baker. Jesus says not to be afraid of those who kill the body “…and after that can do no more.” (Luke 12:4). He's talking to His friends here, and He picks His words carefully. Their reach has an end, and He says where it is.

explanations.answer: They will be judged at once
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that here. After those who kill the body, He says they “…can do no more.” (Luke 12:4). He gives no timing and no verdict on them in this verse. Judged at once is a big claim for a sentence that stops right there.

explanations.answer: They will come to regret it
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a neat ending, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says those who kill the body “…can do no more.” (Luke 12:4). Nothing about regret is in the verse.

explanations.answer: The One with authority to throw them into hell
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him!” (Luke 12:5). He says it plainly, and He even says it twice in a way. This is a heavy part, and I think He wants His friends to hear it clearly.

explanations.answer: The Pharisees who are watching Him closely
explanations.explanation: Jesus mentions the Pharisees back in verse 1, but He doesn't point to them here. He says, “Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell.” (Luke 12:5). The one to fear has authority beyond the killing of the body. That's a different level than any person.

explanations.answer: The rulers who can drag them into court
explanations.explanation: Jesus does mention rulers a few verses later, when He says the disciples will be brought before “…synagogues, rulers, and authorities…” (Luke 12:11). But in this verse He says to fear “…the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell.” (Luke 12:5). That's the one who matters here. I think it helps to keep those two verses separate.
Right, baker. Jesus asks, “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God.” (Luke 12:6). Cheap in the market, not forgotten by God. That's what He says.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says, “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God.” (Luke 12:6). Cheap price, yet not one is forgotten. The price tag doesn't decide that.
Not quite, baker. Jesus says, “So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.” (Luke 12:7). More, not about the same. After the sparrows, He tells His friends where they stand.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.” (Luke 12:7). He just finished saying not one sparrow is forgotten by God, then tells His friends they're worth more than many of them. That's a lot of reasons not to be afraid.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…everyone who confesses Me before men, the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God.” (Luke 12:8). Someone claims Him in front of people, and He claims them in front of the angels of God. I think that's a promise worth holding on to.

Jesus doesn't mention the elders of Israel here. He says the Son of Man “…will also confess him before the angels of God.” (Luke 12:8). The setting He names is the angels of God. Keep your eyes on the verse, friend.

I get why that pick looks good, friend. But Jesus says the Son of Man “…will also confess him before the angels of God.” (Luke 12:8). Confessing Him happens before men, and His confessing them happens before the angels of God. Different rooms, baker.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “But whoever denies Me before men will be denied before the angels of God.” (Luke 12:9). It's the other side of the verse before it. Claiming Him and denying Him both get an answer before the angels of God.

Not quite, friend. Jesus really does say it: “But whoever denies Me before men will be denied before the angels of God.” (Luke 12:9). This is a heavy line, and I won't pretend it isn't. It comes right after the promise about those who confess Him.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.” (Luke 12:10). Just before that, He says everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. That's a serious line, friend.

Moses is a big name, baker, but Jesus doesn't name him here. He says, “…whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.” (Luke 12:10). Even a famous name can't take the Holy Spirit's spot in that sentence.

The prophets aren't named in this verse, friend. Jesus says everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, “…but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.” (Luke 12:10). The Holy Spirit is the one He points to.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say.” (Luke 12:11). He's talking about being brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities. He tells them not to worry, and that's a relief to a nervous talker like me.

Hide is a natural pick when you picture a scary courtroom. But Jesus says, “…do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say.” (Luke 12:11). Earlier He said nothing hidden stays hidden (Luke 12:2). This verse is about defending, friend.

Free sounds like the happy ending, baker, and I'd pick it too. But Jesus says, “…do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say.” (Luke 12:11). Defending is the worry He lifts off them, and I'd gladly hand that one over.
Not quite, baker. Jesus says, “For at that time the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say.” (Luke 12:12). They won't be hunting for words by themselves. The Holy Spirit does the teaching.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “For at that time the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say.” (Luke 12:12). The disciples don't have to cook up the words alone. The Holy Spirit teaches them at that time.
